syntaxCards.note: Min-heap pops the smallest element. Java and C++ compare with greater<int>() and greater<>(). Python heapq is always a min-heap; use negative values for a max-heap.

snippets.python:
import heapq
heapq.heappush(pq, v)   # min-heap
heapq.heappop(pq)    # smallest
# max-heap: push -v, pop, negate

syntaxCards.note: Two pointers need a monotone invariant: if the sum is too small, left must move right; if too large, right must move left. Sorting first is what makes the monotone step valid.
Prefer the lower-bound half-open form. It has no off-by-one branch and returns the first index where the predicate holds.
BFS with a Queue visits in wave order, so the first time you reach a node is its shortest distance. DFS with recursion or a Stack is for reachability and cycle structure, not distance.
Variable-width windows: add the entering element, then shrink while the window is invalid. The shrink condition must reference the same predicate you tested to expand.
When you need to know whether a value was seen before, a HashMap costs O(1) average instead of a Set scan. Reserve capacity when the input size is known to avoid rehashing.
Write the state definition as a sentence before any code. Tabulation fills a table bottom-up; memoisation recurses top-down. Both compute the same states.
A stack gives O(1) push and pop and surfaces the most recent unmatched opener. Use an ArrayDeque in Java rather than a legacy Stack so insertion order is well defined.

snippets.python:
st = []
st.append(c)
o = st.pop()
empty = not st

syntaxCards.note: The choose-recurse-undo cycle is the whole algorithm. Push before recursing and always pop after, in the reverse order of the push, or sibling branches inherit corrupted state.

Recursion mirrors the tree shape. Preorder visits node then children, inorder is required for sorted binary trees, postorder computes values that depend on both subtrees. Depth can exceed the stack limit on skewed trees, so an explicit stack is safer in interviews.

snippets.python:
def preorder(node, out):
    if node is None: return
    out.append(node.val)
    preorder(node.left, out)
    preorder(node.right, out)

syntaxCards.note: x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, which yields a running count of set bits. For a power of two, x & (x - 1) is zero.

snippets.python:
x = n
count = 0
while x:
    x &= x - 1
    count += 1
is_pow2 = n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

syntaxCards.note: For merge problems sort by start time. For sweep problems such as meeting rooms, sort by start and compare each start against a max-heap of end times.
A greedy choice must be locally safe, so it needs a proof: usually an exchange argument showing the greedy pick can be substituted into an optimal solution without loss.
There is no index, so every operation needs a saved pointer. When you remove or reverse a node, capture next before you overwrite it.

snippets.python:
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next
return prev

syntaxCards.note: Sum without the plus operator is XOR plus carry. The carry comes from AND, shifted one place left. Keep adding the carry until it is zero.

snippets.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF
s = (a ^ b) & MASK
carry = ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
while carry:
    s = (s ^ carry) & MASK
    carry = ((s & carry) << 1) & MASK
return s - (1 << 32) if s >> 31 else s

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Each input has exactly one solution and you may not use the same element twice.
problems.keyIdea: Trade a nested scan for a remembered past. Store each value with its index as you go, so the complement of the current value is a single lookup rather than a full search.

ladder.label: Brute force
ladder.why: Check every pair. Correct and obvious, but you scan the rest of the array once per element.

ladder.label: Sorted two pointers
ladder.why: Sorting makes the sum monotone in each cursor, so one pointer can be discarded per step. Sorting dominates the cost.

code.python:
s = sorted(nums)
l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
while l < r:
    if s[l] + s[r] == target: return [l, r]
    if s[l] + s[r] < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1

ladder.label: Hash map single pass
ladder.why: One pass, no sorting. You pay O(n) space to buy back the O(n log n) sort and the second scan.

hints: You need the complement of the current value. What structure makes finding it O(1)?
As you scan left to right, store each value together with its index.
Before storing nums[i], check whether target - nums[i] is already stored. That ordering is what prevents reusing one element.
A HashMap of value to index. One pass over the array.
Pseudocode: for each i, look up need in seen; if found return [seen[need], i]; else seen[nums[i]] = i.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.statement: Given a string containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. An input string is valid if open brackets are closed by the same type of bracket and in the correct order.
problems.keyIdea: Nesting is strictly last-in-first-out, which is exactly what a stack guarantees. Push openers, and every closer must match the most recent unmatched opener.

ladder.label: Rescan on every mismatch
ladder.why: On finding a mismatch, restart validation from the beginning. Correct but re-checks the same prefix repeatedly.

ladder.label: Counting brackets
ladder.why: Counts total openings against closings. It detects a missing or extra bracket but silently accepts '{]}' because the ordering is never checked.

code.python:
opening = sum(s.count(c) for c in '({[')
closing = sum(s.count(c) for c in ')}]')
return opening == closing

ladder.label: Stack with type matching
ladder.why: Push every opener, then require each closer to match the stack top. Ordering becomes structurally enforced rather than counted.

hints: Which data structure matches strict nesting order exactly?
Openers must close in reverse order of opening. That is the definition of a stack.
Push openers. On a closer, the stack top must be its partner, or the string is invalid.
A stack of characters, plus a map from closer to opener.
Pseudocode: push '(' '{' '['; for any closer, if stack empty return false, else pop and compare to its partner; at the end return stack.isEmpty().

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. You can either climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
problems.keyIdea: The ways to reach step i are the ways to reach i-1 plus the ways to reach i-2, because the last move was either one or two steps. That recurrence is Fibonacci.

ladder.label: Tree of all move sequences
ladder.why: Enumerate every possible sequence of 1s and 2s. Exponential because the same subproblem recurs exponentially often.

ladder.label: Memoised recursion
ladder.why: Caching each computed value collapses the exponential recursion into a linear chain. Memoisation with recursion is the top-down form.

ladder.label: Tabulation with two variables
ladder.why: Only the previous two states are ever read, so the whole table collapses to two variables. Same linear time, constant memory.

hints: How many moves reach the final step, and who could have arrived there?
You can only arrive on step i from step i-1 with a one-step move or from step i-2 with a two-step move. Those two cases are disjoint.
Write ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) and then ask how many distinct states exist.
There are n states. A naive recursion recomputes the same states exponentially many times.
Either cache each value (top-down) or fill the values in order from step 1 (bottom-up). Note that only the last two are ever needed.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
problems.keyIdea: The depth of a node is one more than the deeper of its two subtrees. That single recurrence is the entire problem; every approach is just a different way of walking it.

ladder.label: Level order with a queue
ladder.why: Walk the tree one level at a time and count the levels. Simple and immune to recursion limits, but a wide tree holds an entire level in memory at once.

ladder.label: Recursive depth of the taller side
ladder.why: One plus the deeper child is the whole recurrence. It reads as three lines and costs one stack frame per level.

code.java:
if (root == null) return 0;
return 1 + Math.max(depth(root.left), depth(root.right));

ladder.label: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
ladder.why: Same recurrence, but the depth is tracked explicitly instead of living in the call stack. A skewed tree of a hundred thousand nodes will not overflow.

hints: How do you get from the two subtree depths to the depth of their parent?
The path through a node goes through whichever child is deeper. The other child is irrelevant to the answer.
Try writing the answer as one plus the maximum of two recursive calls.
What is the depth of an empty tree? That gives you the base case.
Pseudocode: if node is empty return 0, else return 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).

problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
problems.statement: Write a function that takes an unsigned integer n and returns the number of set bits it has, also called the population count. Assume n is a non-negative 32-bit integer.
problems.keyIdea: x AND (x minus 1) clears the lowest set bit in a single operation. Counting how many times you can do that before the number reaches zero is exactly counting the set bits.

ladder.label: Convert to binary and count characters
ladder.why: Write the number out in base two and count the ones. Understandable, but it allocates a string to answer a question about a fixed 32 bit word.

code.java: return (int) Integer.toBinaryString(n).chars().filter(c -> c == '1').count();
code.python: return bin(n).count('1')

ladder.label: Kernighan's trick
ladder.why: Each x AND (x minus 1) removes exactly one set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit rather than once per bit. No allocation, and it skips every zero position.

code.python:
count = 0
while n:
    n &= n - 1
    count += 1
return count

ladder.label: SWAR popcount with fixed masks
ladder.why: Add, subtract and mask in fixed width steps so each operation accounts for two bits, then four, then eight, then sixteen at once. The count takes a handful of arithmetic steps regardless of the input.

hints: How do you remove exactly one set bit from a number in a single operation?
Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit to zero and everything below it to one. AND with that result keeps only the cleared bit.
If you AND a number with itself minus one, what happens to the number of set bits?
It loses exactly one set bit. So loop that operation and count how many times you can before reaching zero.
Pseudocode: while n is not zero, set n = n AND (n - 1) and increment the counter.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return its new head.
problems.keyIdea: Reversing is the same local pointer swap repeated along the whole list. Keep one pointer to the part already reversed so nothing is lost on the way.

ladder.label: Copy through an array
ladder.why: Read every node into an array, reverse the array, then build a second list from it. Correct, but it allocates two extra n sized structures and never touches the original pointers.

code.python:
vals = []
cur = head
while cur:
    vals.append(cur.val)
    cur = cur.next

dummy = ListNode(0)
for v in reversed(vals):
    dummy.next = ListNode(v, dummy.next)
return dummy.next

ladder.label: Recursive reversal
ladder.why: The recursion stack holds the rest of the list for you, so the code reads as three lines. It costs one stack frame per node, so a list longer than the stack limit will overflow.

code.python:
def reverse(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = reverse(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

ladder.label: Iterative three pointers
ladder.why: The same pointer surgery with no recursion, so the stack never grows with the list. Three pointers and the reversal is done in a single pass.

code.python:
prev, cur = None, head
while cur:
    cur.next, prev, cur = prev, cur, cur.next
return prev

hints: What single pointer change reverses a two node list?
Reversal is local: if a points to b, you want b to point back to a. Each node needs exactly one rewire.
You need a pointer to the node you already reversed, so the next iteration does not lose the finished part.
Keep prev (already reversed), cur (current node) and next (saved before the overwrite).
Pseudocode: while cur: save next, set cur.next to prev, advance prev to cur, advance cur to next. Return prev.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
problems.keyIdea: The window must stay duplicate-free. When a repeat appears, advance the left edge past the previous occurrence rather than restarting the scan.

ladder.label: Check every substring
ladder.why: Enumerate all O(n^2) substrings and verify each with an O(n) set. Quadratic start times linear work.

ladder.label: Sliding window with a set
ladder.why: The outer scan is now linear, but shrinking one character at a time and re-checking the whole window stays quadratic.

code.python:
best = 0; l = 0; seen = set()
for r, ch in enumerate(s):
    while ch in seen:
        seen.remove(s[l]); l += 1
    seen.add(ch)
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)
return best

ladder.label: Sliding window with last-seen map
ladder.why: Remember where each character last appeared. The left edge jumps straight to one past that index instead of creeping forward one character at a time.

hints: What invariant must hold for the current window?
The window can never contain a duplicate. When adding a character that already exists inside it, the left edge must move.
Do not shrink one character at a time. Jump the left edge directly past the previous occurrence of the repeating character.
A map from character to its last seen index. On a repeat, set left to lastSeen[c] + 1.
Pseudocode: for each r, if last[s[r]] >= l then l = last[s[r]] + 1; last[s[r]] = r; best = max(best, r - l + 1).

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: An array sorted in ascending order is rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the rotated array and an integer target, return the index of target if it exists, or -1 if it is not in the array. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
problems.keyIdea: At every split one half is still fully sorted. Identify which half by comparing the midpoint against the low bound, then discard the half that cannot contain the target.

ladder.label: Linear scan
ladder.why: Rotation does not affect membership testing. Ignores the sorted structure entirely and fails the stated complexity requirement.

ladder.label: Binary search then linear wrap
ladder.why: Binary search one monotonic run, then scan the tail. Correct and simple, but the scan makes worst-case behaviour unpredictable.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l <= r:
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if nums[m] == target: return m
    if nums[m] > target: r = m - 1
    else: l = m + 1
return next((i for i, v in enumerate(nums) if v == target), -1)

ladder.label: Modified binary search
ladder.why: At least one half around the midpoint is sorted. Test that half's range against the target and discard the other, halving the window every step.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l <= r:
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if nums[m] == target: return m
    if nums[l] <= nums[m]:
        if nums[l] <= target < nums[m]: r = m - 1
        else: l = m + 1
    else:
        if nums[m] < target <= nums[r]: l = m + 1
        else: r = m - 1
return -1

hints: Why does ordinary binary search break on a rotated array?
Because the array is not globally sorted, the usual discard rule is no longer trustworthy. You need a different signal each step.
At any midpoint, one of the two halves is still sorted. Determine which one by comparing nums[left] to nums[mid].
If the left half is sorted, the target is either inside it or in the right half. If the right half is sorted, the opposite applies.
Pseudocode: if nums[l] <= nums[m] then range-check the left half, else range-check the right half. Narrow one bound each iteration.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.
problems.keyIdea: Build the answer one position at a time. Choose an unused value for the current slot, recurse, then undo the choice so the next branch starts from the same state.

ladder.label: Enumerate all orderings
ladder.why: Generate every arrangement directly. The factorial growth is the problem to be solved, not worked around.

ladder.label: Used-array bookkeeping
ladder.why: Same factorial cost but tracks used values explicitly, which makes the logic portable to problems with duplicate elements.

code.python:
used = [False] * len(nums)
cur = []
def bt():
    if len(cur) == len(nums):
        out.append(cur[:]); return
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if used[i]: continue
        used[i] = True; cur.append(nums[i])
        bt()
        cur.pop(); used[i] = False
bt()

ladder.label: Swap into position, no used array
ladder.why: There is no asymptotic win left, because n! permutations must be materialised. The gain is allocation: this version reuses the input as the working state, so the extra memory is the recursion stack instead of a separate used array plus a fresh list per leaf.

hints: What does one branch of the search tree represent?
A partial arrangement. A complete leaf is a full permutation. You need to grow the branch and then restore it.
At each level, try every value not yet used, recurse, then remove it.
The critical detail is undoing the choice. Without the undo, every sibling sees a corrupted array.
Pseudocode: if the current path is full, record it. Otherwise for each unused value: push it, recurse, pop it.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.statement: You are given an integer array nums. Each element nums[i] represents the maximum jump length available at that position. Start at index 0 and return true if you can reach the last index, or false if it is not possible.
problems.keyIdea: Track the furthest index reachable so far. If the current index passes that frontier, no choice of path could have helped, because the frontier is the best any earlier jump could have bought.

ladder.label: Try every path
ladder.why: Recursively try every jump length from every position. Exponential, because the same suffix is re-explored exponentially many times.

ladder.label: Dynamic programming from the end
ladder.why: Mark every index you can reach, working backwards. Linear time, but it keeps a boolean per index when the answer only ever needs one running number.

ladder.label: Greedy furthest reach
ladder.why: One variable holds the furthest index reachable. If the current index ever passes it, the answer is no. Constant space, single pass, and no array of states.

hints: Do you need to know every reachable position, or just the furthest one?
If you can reach index 9, every index up to 9 is also reachable. Reachability is a prefix, not a scattered set.
Keep a single number: the furthest index anything so far can jump to.
At each index, extend the frontier with i plus nums[i]. If the frontier falls behind the current index, you are stuck.
Pseudocode: reach = 0. For each i, if i > reach return false, else reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]).

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.statement: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] equals start i and end i, merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the input ranges.
problems.keyIdea: Sort by start time, then sweep once. Each interval either extends the run you are building or has to begin a new one, and no interval can ever overlap something more than one position behind.

ladder.label: Repeated pairwise merging until stable
ladder.why: Keep merging any two overlapping intervals until nothing changes. Correct, but it rescans the entire list after every single merge.

ladder.label: Sort by start, then one merge pass
ladder.why: Sorting by start makes every overlap adjacent, so a single left to right pass finishes the job. It still allocates a second n sized array.

ladder.label: In-place merge into the same array
ladder.why: Same sorted sweep, but the result is written back over the input as it goes. The only extra memory is whatever the sort itself needs.

hints: What makes two intervals adjacent in the list rather than scattered?
Sorting. Once intervals are ordered by start, an interval can only overlap the one you are currently building or the one right after it.
Sort by start time, then walk once comparing each start against the current run's end.
If start is at or before the current end, extend the end. Otherwise push a new interval.
Pseudocode: sort by start. For each interval, if it overlaps the last merged one, extend that one's end, else append it.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.statement: Given an m x n 2D binary grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (waters), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.
problems.keyIdea: Each new unvisited land cell starts exactly one island. Flood-fill the whole connected component so it is never counted twice.

ladder.label: Repeated flood fill without marking
ladder.why: The fill explores the same component from every starting cell because nothing records that ground was already processed.

ladder.label: Flood fill with visited set
ladder.why: An explicit visited set makes the complexity provably linear, at the cost of auxiliary memory alongside the grid.

ladder.label: Iterative sink as you count
ladder.why: The sink writes its own state, so no auxiliary structure is needed. Same asymptotics as the visited set, but O(1) extra memory.

hints: How do you avoid counting one island twice?
When you find unvisited land, that cell must be the start of a brand new island. Once counted, the whole connected region is finished.
Flood fill from the starting cell, marking every land cell you touch so the outer loop skips it.
Recursive DFS is simplest but can overflow the stack on large grids. An explicit stack keeps memory on the heap.
Pseudocode: on unvisited '1', increment the count, then flood fill all connected '1' cells, marking each as '0' as you visit it.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. It is not necessarily the kth distinct element.
problems.keyIdea: You only ever need the top k values, so anything outside that set is dead weight. Discarding the rest is what turns a full sort into a partial one.

ladder.label: Sort and index from the end
ladder.why: Sort ascending and read index n minus k. Always correct, but it totally orders every element in order to use k of them.

code.python: return sorted(nums, reverse=True)[k - 1]

ladder.label: Quickselect around a pivot
ladder.why: Partition around a pivot so everything larger goes to one side, then recurse only into the side holding position k. Average linear, but the worst case degenerates to n squared when the pivot keeps landing on an extreme.

code.python:
def quick_select(a, lo, hi, target):
    while lo < hi:
        pivot = a[(lo + hi) // 2]
        i, j = lo, hi
        while i <= j:
            while a[i] < pivot: i += 1
            while a[j] > pivot: j -= 1
            if i <= j:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1; j -= 1
        if target <= j: hi = j
        elif target >= i: lo = i
        else: return

a = list(nums)
quick_select(a, 0, len(a) - 1, len(a) - k)
return a[len(a) - k]

ladder.label: Min-heap of size k
ladder.why: Keep only the k largest in a min-heap. The heap top is always the smallest of the current top k, so it is exactly the next value to evict. Cost depends on k, not on n.

code.python:
import heapq

pq = []
for v in nums:
    heapq.heappush(pq, v)
    if len(pq) > k:
        heapq.heappop(pq)
return pq[0]

hints: How many values do you actually need to remember at any moment?
Only k. Every other element is irrelevant the moment you read it.
If you kept the k largest seen so far, what structure answers which one to throw away?
A min-heap of size k. Its top is the smallest of the k largest, so that is the one that gets evicted.
Pseudocode: push each value, and whenever the heap size exceeds k, pop it. The heap top at the end is the answer.

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.statement: Given two integers a and b, return the sum of the two integers without using the plus or minus operators.
problems.keyIdea: XOR gives the sum without any carry. AND identifies exactly the positions that produce a carry, and shifting that left by one moves the carry into the next position.

ladder.label: Add one bit position at a time
ladder.why: Walk all 32 positions individually, writing the sum bit into the result and shifting the carry up by hand each round. Correct but mechanical, and it always does exactly 32 iterations.

code.python:
result = 0
carry = 0
for i in range(32):
    a_bit = (a >> i) & 1
    b_bit = (b >> i) & 1
    sum_bit = a_bit ^ b_bit ^ carry
    carry = a_bit & b_bit | (a_bit & carry) | (b_bit & carry)
    result |= sum_bit << i
return result

ladder.label: XOR for the sum, AND for the carry
ladder.why: XOR already computes the sum of each bit pair ignoring carries, and AND marks exactly the positions that carry. Shift the carry left and feed it back until it disappears. Usually converges in two or three rounds.

code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF

total = (a ^ b) & MASK
carry = ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
while carry:
    total = (total ^ carry) & MASK
    carry = ((total & carry) << 1) & MASK

return total - (1 << 32) if total >> 31 else total

ladder.label: Branchless fixed-width carry propagation
ladder.why: Identical arithmetic, but the loop always runs 32 times with no data dependent exit. On a fixed width word the answer is identical while the branch becomes fully predictable, which is what you want in hot code.

code.python:
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF

total = (a ^ b) & MASK
carry = (a & b) & MASK
for _ in range(32):
    total, carry = (total ^ carry) & MASK, ((total & carry) << 1) & MASK

return total - (1 << 32) if total >> 31 else total

hints: Which bitwise operator gives you 1 only where exactly one input bit is 1?
XOR. That is the sum of a bit pair when you ignore carrying entirely.
Which operator identifies the positions where a carry will actually be produced?
AND, shifted one place left. That carry then has to be added back into the sum, which means feeding it through the same XOR step again.
Pseudocode: sum = a XOR b, carry = a AND b. While carry is nonzero: next = (sum AND carry) shifted left, sum = sum XOR carry, carry = next.
